q.q: The vendor sends fix-12.patch, made with `diff -ru` for the source tree. You are inside the unpacked directory. Which command applies it?
o: tar -xf ../fix-12.patch
A patch file is a text diff, not an archive.
install -m 755 ../fix-12.patch .
install copies a file with chosen permissions and does not apply changes.
patch -p1 < ../fix-12.patch
Right. patch reads the diff from standard input. -p1 strips the first directory level from the file names in the patch so they match your tree.
make patch
make has no built-in patch target unless the project defines one.

q.q: If you run ./configure with no options and then `make install`, where do the program files go by default?
o: Under /opt
/opt is used only when you set --prefix=/opt/... yourself.
Under /usr/local, for example /usr/local/bin
Right. The default prefix is /usr/local. This keeps locally built software apart from packages managed by the distribution.
Under /home/<user>
The home directory is used only when the prefix is changed to it.
Under /usr, mixed with distribution packages
/usr is for the package manager, and configure does not use it unless you ask.

q.q: Which set of directories is the best to EXCLUDE from a full-system file backup because they are virtual or rebuilt at every boot?
o: /proc, /sys, /dev and /run
Right. These hold live kernel and device information, not stored data. Always include /etc, /home and data directories such as /var/lib.
/boot and /usr/local
Both hold files that are not rebuilt automatically and need saving.
/root and /srv
Root's files and served data are not regenerated.
/etc, /home and /var/lib
These hold configuration, user data and databases, so they must be kept.

q.q: The plan is a full backup on Sunday and incremental backups Monday to Wednesday. The disk fails Thursday morning. What do you restore, in order?
o: Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday incrementals, without the full
Without the full backup there is no base to apply them to.
Only Wednesday's incremental
It has just that day's changes, and not the base data.
Sunday's full backup and only Wednesday's incremental
That would work for a differential plan, but here Monday and Tuesday changes would be missing.
Sunday's full plus Mon, Tue and Wed incrementals in order
Right. An incremental holds changes since the previous backup of any kind, so every link of the chain is needed. A differential would need only the full plus the latest one.

q.q: `rsync -a /srv/data /backup` is run once. What ends up in /backup?
o: An error, because rsync always needs a remote host
rsync works locally as well.
Nothing, because -a only works together with --delete
-a is archive mode and works alone.
A directory /backup/data with all the files in it
Right. Without the trailing slash, rsync copies the directory itself. With /srv/data/ it would copy only the contents into /backup.
The contents of /srv/data placed directly in /backup
That is what a trailing slash on the source would do.

q.q: Which command makes a raw image of the whole disk /dev/sda into a file on a mounted backup drive?
o: dd if=/dev/sda of=/mnt/backup/sda.img bs=4M
Right. if is the input and of is the output. Swapping them would overwrite the disk with the file, so double-check before pressing Enter.
cp /dev/sda /dev/null
That copies the disk to nowhere and makes no image.
dd if=/mnt/backup/sda.img of=/dev/sda bs=4M
This reverses the direction and would overwrite the disk with the file.
tar -cf /dev/sda /mnt/backup/sda.img
tar would write an archive onto the disk device and destroy it.

q.q: What is the strongest way to check that a backup is good?
o: Confirm the backup drive is still plugged in
That shows the drive is present, not that the data is good.
Do a test restore and compare checksums
Right. Only a test restore proves the data can really be read back. Listing an archive (tar -tzf) and checking its checksum are useful but weaker.
Check that the backup job exits with status 0
A clean exit does not prove the files are complete or readable.
Look at the file size of the archive
A size alone cannot show whether contents are intact.

q.q: You write several tar archives one after another on the same tape with `mt` and tar. Which device name keeps the tape from rewinding after each archive?
o: /dev/st0
st0 rewinds the tape when the program ends, so the next write starts at the beginning.
/dev/tape-fast
There is no such standard device name.
/dev/sda0
sda is a disk device, not a tape drive.
/dev/nst0
Right. The n in nst0 stands for non-rewinding. /dev/st0 rewinds when closed, so the next archive would overwrite the first.

q.q: You want a legal notice shown to SSH users AFTER they log in successfully. Which file holds it?
o: /etc/issue
It is displayed before login on the console, not after login.
/etc/hosts.allow
That file controls which hosts may reach services.
/etc/motd
Right. motd (message of the day) is printed after login. /etc/issue is shown before login on local consoles, and /etc/issue.net is used for network logins that call for a banner.
/etc/fstab
fstab lists filesystems to mount.

q.q: Maintenance requires a reboot in 30 minutes, and logged-in users should be warned automatically with a message. Which command does it?
o: shutdown -r +30 "Patching tonight"
Right. shutdown with a time sends a warning to all terminals, blocks new logins shortly before the time, and can be cancelled with shutdown -c.
wall "Rebooting in 30 minutes"
wall only broadcasts text. It schedules nothing.
reboot --wtmp-only
-w writes a record to the wtmp log and does not reboot or warn anyone.
systemctl reboot --message="30 minutes"
systemctl reboot acts at once, and it has no such delay option.

q.title: Fix a data disk that sends the server into emergency mode
q.scenario: After a planned reboot, app04 stops in emergency mode and the /data volume is not mounted. Find out why, correct the problem in /etc/fstab, and prove that every fstab entry mounts. Do not erase the disk, and do not simply delete the /data line.

checks.t: Read why /data failed (status or journal)
checks.why: Both show 'Timed out waiting for device /dev/disk/by-uuid/...3f18'. systemd was looking for a disk with that exact UUID and never found it, so the /data mount failed and the boot fell into emergency mode.

checks.t: Look up the real UUID of /dev/sdb1
checks.why: blkid (or lsblk -f) lists the UUID the disk really has. It ends in ...0f81, but fstab asks for ...0f18: two digits are swapped.

checks.t: Read the /data line in /etc/fstab
checks.why: You must compare what fstab asks for with what blkid reports. The typo is in the UUID on the /data line.

checks.t: Correct the UUID after remounting / read-write
checks.why: Emergency mode mounts / read-only, so an edit fails until you run mount -o remount,rw /. Only after that can the corrected line be saved.

checks.t: Prove it with mount -a after the fix
checks.why: mount -a tries every fstab entry that is not mounted yet. Running it after the fix and getting no error shows the entries are valid.

checks.t: Did not delete the /data line
checks.why: Removing the line hides the error, but the application would then write into the root filesystem and fill it. The right fix is to correct the UUID.

checks.t: Did not format the disk
checks.why: The disk and its XFS data are fine. mkfs would erase everything. Only the UUID text in fstab was wrong.

checks.t: Confirm the array is degraded and find the failed member
checks.why: /proc/mdstat shows sdc1 marked (F) and [U_]. mdadm --detail says 'clean, degraded' with one faulty device. This tells you which partition to remove.

checks.t: Remove the failed member sdc1
checks.why: A failed member must be removed from the array before a new one takes its place. mdadm /dev/md0 --remove /dev/sdc1 does that (--fail is already done by the kernel).

checks.t: Add /dev/sdd1 after the removal
checks.why: Adding the replacement starts the rebuild at once. Removing the failed disk first keeps the array's member list clean.

checks.t: Check that the rebuild is running
checks.why: Look again after adding. A 'recovery = ...%' line in /proc/mdstat, or 'spare rebuilding' in mdadm --detail, proves the mirror is being rebuilt.

checks.t: Save the array in mdadm.conf
checks.why: mdadm --detail --scan prints an ARRAY line. Appending it to /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf makes the system assemble the array as /dev/md0 and not as /dev/md127.

checks.t: Did not run mdadm --create
checks.why: --create makes a brand-new array and can overwrite the metadata of the live one. Repairs use --remove and --add.

checks.t: Did not zero the superblock of the healthy disk
checks.why: --zero-superblock erases the array information from a disk. On sdb1 it would remove the only good copy from the array.

checks.t: Read the routing table
checks.why: ip route lists only 192.0.2.0/24 and has no 'default via ...' line. Without a default route the host has no next hop for any other network, which is why it reports 'Network is unreachable'.

checks.t: Check that the gateway answers on the local subnet
checks.why: A successful ping to 192.0.2.1 proves the cable, address and ARP all work. The gateway is reachable, so only the route is missing.

checks.t: Add the default route through 192.0.2.1
checks.why: ip route add default via 192.0.2.1 gives the host a next hop for every network not in its table. The gateway must be on the local subnet, as here.

checks.t: Test a remote host after adding the route
checks.why: Always verify the fix: a ping to 198.51.100.10 that now works proves traffic leaves the subnet. Testing before the fix only shows the failure again.

checks.t: Make the gateway permanent in NetworkManager
checks.why: ip route add changes only the running system. nmcli connection modify writes the gateway into the profile, so it is applied again after a reboot or restart of the connection.

checks.t: Did not flush the interface address
checks.why: The address is correct. Flushing it would remove it and cut your remote session, and it does nothing about the missing route.

checks.t: Did not take the interface down
checks.why: The link works, as the gateway ping shows. Bringing it down would end your session and would not add the route.

q.title: Read dmesg: why did wlan0 disappear after the kernel update?
q.scenario: After a kernel update and reboot, a field laptop no longer shows its wireless interface wlan0 in ip link. The wired port works. Read these lines from dmesg and mark every line that points to the problem, then say what the log shows.
q.ticket: INC-6155: laptop WL-22 (Debian 12, kernel 6.1.0-22). Wi-Fi worked on kernel 6.1.0-18. The kernel package was updated. Nothing else was changed.

lines.text: [    1.204511] usb 1-3: new high-speed USB device number 3 using xhci_hcd
lines.why: The kernel found a USB device (a built-in camera or hub). This is normal startup noise and has nothing to do with Wi-Fi.

lines.text: [    2.019873] e1000e 0000:00:1f.6 eno1: NIC Link is Up 1000 Mbps Full Duplex, Flow Control: None
lines.why: The wired network card loaded its driver and has a link. That matches the report that the wired port works.
The wireless driver iwlwifi found the card and switched it on. This is the normal first step, so it is not a fault by itself.

lines.text: [    2.355907] iwlwifi 0000:00:14.3: Direct firmware load for iwlwifi-so-a0-gf-a0-83.ucode failed with error -2
lines.why: Error -2 is 'no such file'. The driver asked for a firmware file and the file is not on disk. This is the first sign of the problem.
The driver stops here because it cannot use any firmware version it supports, so no wlan0 is created.
This names the oldest firmware the new driver accepts. The system lacks it, so the linux-firmware package is too old or missing for this card.

lines.text: [    3.801662] EXT4-fs (nvme0n1p2): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode. Quota mode: none.
lines.why: The root filesystem mounted normally, so storage is fine.

lines.text: [    5.120034] Bluetooth: hci0: Bootloader revision 0.4 build 0 week 11 2015
lines.why: The Bluetooth part of the card reports in. It does not load the Wi-Fi firmware and is not an error.

ask.label: What does this log show?
opts: A udev rule renamed wlan0 to a different interface name
The kernel was built without the iwlwifi module
The wireless driver loaded but the firmware file it needs is missing
The Wi-Fi radio is switched off by a hardware rfkill switch
ask.why: The log shows iwlwifi loading, then failing to find its .ucode firmware file ('failed with error -2', 'no suitable firmware found'). A renamed interface would still exist and the driver would not report missing firmware. A kernel without the module would show no iwlwifi lines at all. An rfkill switch leaves the interface present but blocked. The fix is to install or update firmware-iwlwifi (Debian) or linux-firmware (RHEL/Fedora) and reload the module.

q.title: Grow a full logical volume with a new disk
q.scenario: The ext4 logical volume that holds /var/www is full. Volume group vg_data has no free extents left. A new empty disk, /dev/sdd, was just installed. Build the safe steps that make /var/www 100 GB larger while the website stays online. Put the needed steps in order and leave out the harmful or useless ones.
q.ticket: Volume group vg_data, logical volume lv_www (ext4, mounted at /var/www). The new disk has no partitions and no data.

rules.why: Writes an LVM label on the new disk so it becomes a physical volume. Only physical volumes can be added to a volume group.
Adds the new physical volume to the existing group. This gives vg_data free extents it can hand to lv_www.
Makes the logical volume 100 GB bigger. The filesystem inside does not grow by itself yet.
Grows the ext4 filesystem to fill the larger logical volume. ext4 can be grown while mounted, so the site stays online.
This creates a new empty filesystem and destroys all the website's files. Growing never needs a new filesystem.
The group vg_data already exists, so this fails. Even with a new name it would make a separate pool and not add space to the existing group.
Not needed. ext4 can be grown online, and unmounting would take the website down for no reason.
This shrinks the volume, the opposite of the goal. Shrinking a volume without shrinking the filesystem first destroys data.

before.why: vgextend only accepts a physical volume, so the disk must be prepared with pvcreate first.
lvextend can take space only from free extents in the group. Those do not exist until vgextend adds the new disk.
resize2fs grows the filesystem to the size of the logical volume. The volume must be larger first, or there is nothing to grow into.

last.why: Growing the filesystem is the final step. Until then, df still shows the old size, even though the volume is larger.

q.title: Place the stages of a UEFI Linux boot, in order
q.scenario: A server with UEFI firmware is powered on and boots Linux with GRUB 2 and a systemd-based distribution. Place each stage in the order it happens, from the power button to the running system. Knowing the order tells you where to look when a boot fails.

devs.name: UEFI firmware (hardware check)
devs.why: The firmware runs first. It tests the hardware and reads its boot entries to decide which EFI program to start. efibootmgr edits those entries.

devs.name: Boot loader on the ESP (shim, then GRUB)
devs.why: The firmware loads an EFI program from the EFI System Partition (usually mounted at /boot/efi). That program is shim and GRUB, which show the menu.

devs.name: Kernel and initramfs loaded into RAM
devs.why: GRUB reads the kernel and the initramfs from /boot, loads them into memory and hands control to the kernel with its command line.

devs.name: Initramfs mounts the real root
devs.why: The initramfs holds the early drivers (storage, LVM, RAID). It finds the root filesystem and mounts it. A failure here gives 'Unable to mount root fs'.

devs.name: systemd (PID 1) starts services
devs.why: Once root is mounted, the kernel starts /sbin/init, which is systemd. It mounts the rest from fstab and brings up services up to the default target.

devs.name: MBR boot code in the first 512 bytes
devs.why: MBR boot code is how legacy BIOS starts. A UEFI machine reads the ESP instead and does not run the MBR code.

devs.name: getty login prompt
devs.why: The login prompt appears after systemd has reached its target, so it comes after all five stages, not as one of them.

devs.name: mkinitrd or dracut run
devs.why: These tools build an initramfs when a kernel is installed or updated. They are not run at power on.
